prompt: In `function-scope.js`, why could `console.log(label)` read `label` after the `if` had closed?
hint: Which keyword declared it?

choices.text: The `if` condition was true, so its names stay alive
choices.why: `shelf` was declared in the same true `if` and was gone.

choices.text: It was a `var`, which belongs to the whole function
choices.why: Right. `var` ignores blocks.

choices.text: `console.log` can see names from any block
choices.why: The same call could not see `shelf`.

choices.text: Strings live longer than numbers
choices.why: Lifetime does not depend on the type of the value.

prompt: Why did `redeclare.js` never print `first line`?
hint: When is a syntax error found?

choices.text: `console.log` is not allowed to run before a `var` declaration in the same file
choices.why: Order of statements was not the problem.

choices.text: Redeclaring `var copies` stopped the program
choices.why: Redeclaring a `var` is allowed.

choices.text: The second `let title` is a syntax error, found before anything runs
choices.why: Right. The file is read whole first, so the program never started.

choices.text: `head -n 5` cut that line off the output
choices.why: The first five lines shown are all about the error; nothing was printed before it.

prompt: Two loops one after the other each use `let i`. How many variables called `i` are there?
hint: Each loop has its own block.

choices.text: One, shared by both loops
choices.why: That is what `var` would give.

choices.text: At least two, one per loop and in fact one per turn
choices.why: Right. Block scope keeps them apart, and the loop section shows one per turn.

choices.text: None, since `i` is created by the engine
choices.why: `let i` is an ordinary declaration.

choices.text: A `SyntaxError`, because `i` is declared twice
choices.why: The two declarations are in different blocks, so they do not collide.

prompt: `console.log(title); var title = "Iracema";` What does the first line print?
hint: A `var` is created before any line runs.

choices.text: `undefined`
choices.why: Right. The name exists, and its value is assigned on line 2.

choices.text: `Iracema`
choices.why: The assignment stays on its own line.

choices.text: `ReferenceError: title is not defined`
choices.why: The `var` declaration was hoisted, so the name is defined.

choices.text: `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'title' before initialization`
choices.why: That is what `let` would give.

prompt: Why did `later()` fail with `TypeError: later is not a function` while `greet("ana")` worked, though both were called before their definitions?
hint: One is a declaration, the other a `var` holding a function.

choices.text: `later` is an arrow function, which cannot be hoisted
choices.why: `later` is a function expression; the `var` holding it is what matters.

choices.text: A `var` is hoisted as `undefined`; a function declaration with its body
choices.why: Right. `later` held `undefined` when it was called.

choices.text: Only the first function in a file is hoisted
choices.why: Every function declaration is hoisted.

choices.text: `greet` was called with an argument and `later` was not
choices.why: Arguments have nothing to do with hoisting.

prompt: Match each declaration with what its name holds before its own line runs.
hint: The table at the end of the section.
right_distractors: The value on the right of `=`

prompt: What does `Cannot access 'title' before initialization` tell you that `title is not defined` does not?
hint: One is an ordering problem.

choices.text: That `title` is misspelt somewhere
choices.why: A typo gives `is not defined`.

choices.text: That `title` was declared with `var` somewhere above the line that read it
choices.why: A `var` would have given `undefined`.

choices.text: That `title` is declared in this scope and its line has not run yet
choices.why: Right. Move the use below the declaration.

choices.text: That `title` holds `null`
choices.why: A name in the dead zone holds nothing at all.

prompt: `console.log(typeof title); let title = "Iracema";` What happens?
hint: Is `typeof` safe in the dead zone?

choices.text: It prints `undefined`, as `typeof` does for any unknown name
choices.why: `title` is not unknown; it is in its dead zone.

choices.text: It prints `string`
choices.why: The assignment has not run yet.

choices.text: It throws a `ReferenceError`
choices.why: Right. Inside the dead zone, `typeof` is a read like any other.

choices.text: It prints `object`
choices.why: Nothing about the value is known yet.

prompt: In `shadow.js`, a `const year = 1899` sits outside `check`, yet `console.log(year)` inside `check` threw. Why?
hint: Where is the inner `year` created?

choices.text: `const` names cannot be read inside functions
choices.why: Functions read outer `const` names all the time.

choices.text: The outer `year` was not yet initialised when `check` ran
choices.why: `check()` runs on line 8, long after line 1.

choices.text: The inner `year` covers the outer one from the top of the body, and line 4 is in its dead zone
choices.why: Right: shadowing begins at the opening brace.

choices.text: Declaring the same name twice is a `SyntaxError`
choices.why: In different scopes it is allowed, and the error was a `ReferenceError`.

prompt: A name in an inner scope that covers the same name in an outer scope is said to ___ it.
hint: The section's word for it.

prompt: `loop-var.js` printed `var 3` three times. Why 3?
hint: When did the callbacks run, and how many `i` are there?

choices.text: `setTimeout` adds 3 to every number it prints
choices.why: It prints nothing itself; the callback reads `i`.

choices.text: The loop ran three extra times after the condition `i < 3` had become false
choices.why: It ran three times, and stopped when `i` reached 3.

choices.text: One `i` for the whole loop, and the callbacks ran after it reached 3
choices.why: Right: they read the variable, not its old value.

choices.text: `var` turns numbers into constants
choices.why: `var` names can be reassigned, which is how `i` got to 3.

prompt: What makes `loop-let.js` print 0, 1 and 2?
hint: Look at the right half of the figure.

choices.text: `let` makes `setTimeout` run immediately
choices.why: The callbacks still ran after the loop.

choices.text: `let` copies the value into each callback
choices.why: A callback keeps a variable; with `let` there are three of them.

choices.text: Each turn of the loop gets its own `i`
choices.why: Right. Three variables, each still holding its turn's number.

choices.text: The loop runs backwards with `let`
choices.why: The order is the same; only the bindings differ.

prompt: In the `var` loop, how many distinct variables named `i` existed?
hint: The left half of the figure.

prompt: You find `(function (j) { … })(i)` inside a `for (var i …)` loop in an old codebase. What is the section's advice?
hint: It is an old fix for a known bug.

choices.text: Keep it: removing it would break the loop
choices.why: Only if `var` stays; the section replaces both.

choices.text: Switch the loop to `let` and delete the wrapper
choices.why: Right. `let` gives one variable per turn, which is all the wrapper did.

choices.text: Replace `setTimeout` with a direct call
choices.why: That changes when the work happens, which was the point of the code.

choices.text: Rename `j` to `i` so the two agree
choices.why: The name does not matter; one variable per turn does.

prompt: In a browser's classic script, which top-level declaration becomes a property of `window`?
hint: `window.readerName` was `undefined`.

choices.text: `var shelfCount = 12`
choices.why: Right, and so does a function declaration.

choices.text: `let readerName = "ana"`
choices.why: It is shared between scripts, but not as a property of `window`.

choices.text: `const MAX = 10`
choices.why: Like `let`, it stays off `window`.

choices.text: None of them; `window` is read-only
choices.why: `window.shelfCount` printed 12.

prompt: A page declares `var name = 42;` at the top of a script. What does `typeof name` give?
hint: `window.name` already exists.

choices.text: `number`, since that is what was assigned
choices.why: The browser's `window.name` keeps only strings.

choices.text: `string`
choices.why: Right. The page printed `string 42`.

choices.text: `undefined`, since the assignment was refused
choices.why: The assignment happened, and the value was converted.

choices.text: A `TypeError`, because `name` is reserved
choices.why: No error was raised, which is what makes it dangerous.

prompt: Why did `globalThis.shelfCount` print `undefined` in Node, after `var shelfCount = 12` at the top of the file?
hint: Lesson 9 explains where that scope comes from.

choices.text: Node does not have a global object
choices.why: It has one, called `globalThis` there as everywhere.

choices.text: The `var` was hoisted and never assigned
choices.why: The assignment ran on line 1.

choices.text: Each Node file has its own scope, so the `var` stays in the file
choices.why: Right. A browser module behaves the same way.

choices.text: `globalThis` is only filled in after the program ends
choices.why: It is there from the start.

prompt: In `implicit.js`, assigning `total = 7` to a name nobody declared created a property on the ___ object.
hint: `globalThis.total` printed 7.

prompt: Put what happens in order for `{ console.log(x); let x = 1; console.log(x); }`.
hint: Hoisting happens before any line runs.
items: The engine creates `x` for the block, uninitialised
The rest of the block never runs

prompt: A colleague asks why the team bans `var`. Which of these does the lesson NOT give as a reason?
hint: Three behaviours differ; one claim here is about speed.

choices.text: It ignores blocks, so a loop's counter leaks into the function
choices.why: The lesson gives this one.

choices.text: Read too early, it gives `undefined` instead of an error
choices.why: The lesson gives this one.

choices.text: At the top of a classic script it collides with properties of `window`
choices.why: The lesson gives this one.

choices.text: It makes the program run more slowly
choices.why: Right: the lesson says nothing about speed. Its reasons are all about wrong values that raise no error.
